states that every graph with chromatic number kk contains a complete graph on kk vertices as a minor. This conjecture is a tremendous strengthening of the Four-Colour Theorem and is regarded as one of the most important open problems in graph theory. The case of Hadwiger’s Conjecture for graphs with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2 has garnered much attention. Seymour writes: “My own belief is, if Hadwiger’s Conjecture is true for graphs with stability number two then it is probably true in general, so it would be very nice to decide this case.”
    

This paper presents several tools useful for proving that a graph GG with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2 satisfies Hadwiger’s Conjecture. In doing so, we survey and generalise several classical results on the α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2 case of Hadwiger’s Conjecture. Further, we apply these tools to prove variants of Hadwiger’s Conjecture for several noteworthy classes of graphs with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2. In particular, we prove Hadwiger’s Conjecture for inflations of the complements of the following graphs: graphs with girth at least 55, triangle-free Kneser graphs, and the Clebsch, Mesner, and Gewirtz graphs.
This paper also highlights classes of graphs with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2 where it is unknown if Hadwiger’s Conjecture holds.
  




1 Introduction




A graph HH is a minor of a graph GG if HH can be obtained from GG by deleting vertices and edges, and by contracting edges. The maximum integer nn such that the complete graph KnK_{n} is a minor of GG is called the Hadwiger number of GG, denoted had⁡(G)\had(G). A proper colouring of a graph GG assigns a colour to each vertex so that adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. The chromatic number of GG, denoted χ⁡(G)\chi(G), is the minimum integer kk such that GG has a proper colouring with kk colours. For any undefined graph theory notation, see Diestel [29]11

α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2, Theorem 1.1 implies that had⁡(G)⩾|V⁡(G)|/3\had(G)\geqslant|V(G)|/3, and Theorem 1.2 does not offer a better bound. However, in this case Conjecture 2 asserts that had⁡(G)⩾|V⁡(G)|/2\had(G)\geqslant|V(G)|/2. This gap is large, and thus the restriction of Hadwiger’s Conjecture to graphs with independence number 22 is interesting. Seymour [57] writes “My own belief is, if Hadwiger’s Conjecture is true for graphs with stability number two then it is probably true in general, so it would be very nice to decide this case”. For convenience, we denote this special case as Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2})..



Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2}).



For every graph GG with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2, had⁡(G)⩾χ⁡(G)\had(G)\geqslant\chi(G).





Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2}). is a key open case of Hadwiger’s Conjecture [53, 22, 7, 19, 11, 49]. Every graph GG with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2 has χ⁡(G)⩾|V⁡(G)|/2\chi(G)\geqslant|V(G)|/2, but the weakening of Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2}). remains open:



Conjecture 4 (HCn/2\HC_{n/2}).



For every graph GG with α⁡(G)=2\alpha(G)=2, had⁡(G)⩾|V⁡(G)|/2\had(G)\geqslant|V(G)|/2.





Plummer et al. [53] proved that a minimum counterexample (in terms of |V⁡(G)||V(G)|) to Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2}). has several properties (see Table 1). In particular, they proved that if GG is a minimum counterexample to Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2})., then diam⁡(G¯)=2\diam(\overline{G})=2, and GG is a counterexample to Conjecture 4 (HCn/2\HC_{n/2}).. Therefore, Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2}). and Conjecture 4 (HCn/2\HC_{n/2}). are equivalent. (Several authors ([11, Theorem 1.2], [66, Theorem 1.3]) have misinterpreted this statement as claiming that every graph that satisfies Conjecture 4 (HCn/2\HC_{n/2}). also satisfies Conjecture 3 (HCα=2\HC_{\alpha=2})..
